now.text: My work connects clinical sequence modelling, tools for scientific discovery, and research software. The common aim is to make complex evidence more useful for medical research.

sections.title: Clinical sequence modelling
sections.description: Understanding patterns in electronic health records and their value for medical research.

projects.title: ASCEND: generative models of patient records
projects.summary: Transformer models that learn how patients’ health records unfold over time, used to study risk, treatment response and patterns of disease.
projects.aim: To build models of routine electronic health records that can forecast a patient’s future care — diagnoses, prescriptions and laboratory values, and when they occur — and that can be asked what would be expected to happen if a different treatment were started. If such a model reproduces known drug effects from observational data, it becomes a single tool for studying treatment response across many drugs and outcomes, including questions that trials have not addressed.
projects.approach: Each patient’s record is represented as a time-stamped sequence of coded events and measurements. ASCENDgpt (2025) used phenotype-aware tokens and an encoder model for cardiovascular risk prediction. FlatASCEND (2026) moved to a compact autoregressive generator that predicts both the next event and its timing, and tested whether simulated treatment starts reproduce known pharmacological associations; a companion study used sparse autoencoders to decompose the model’s internal representations into interpretable clinical features. Current work (ASCEND-GEN) trains one generative model on UK primary-care records and evaluates it against target-trial-style emulations of drug starts across 15 drug classes and six routine outcomes (HbA1c, blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, eGFR, weight and potassium). Rather than fitting a separate model for each question, it builds time-dependent drug-response dynamics into the model itself.

projects.title: ORCA: health records as a language
projects.summary: Treating coded health records as a language, so that clinical sequences from different health systems can be read, compared and translated.
projects.aim: Coded health records are produced jointly by clinicians, laboratories and administrative processes. ORCA asks whether these sequences behave like a language, with measurable statistical structure, and whether that structure can be used to align records from different health systems and to translate between coded records and plain English. A shared, system-independent representation of clinical situations would make it easier to compare populations, transfer models between settings and interpret what a model has learned.
projects.approach: The first phase applied tools from computational linguistics and information theory — frequency and entropy analysis, cross-system alignment, and translation between coded sequences and English — to sequence models trained on records from several health systems. The current phase (ORCA-JEPA) trains joint-embedding predictive (JEPA-style) models on natively coded records from UK and US health systems together, without telling the model which codes mean the same thing. It tests whether patients in the same clinical situation land in the same region of the shared representation whichever system recorded them, using held-out code mappings only as a check, comparison groups matched on age, sex and amount of data, and links to clinical text.

projects.title: Phenotype fingerprinting
projects.summary: Using patterns in clinical records to find patients with rare or under-recognised conditions earlier.
projects.aim: Many clinically important conditions are rare, inconsistently coded or recognised late. The aim is to identify patients with under-recognised phenotypes earlier, starting from small, carefully characterised case sets rather than large labelled cohorts.
projects.approach: Expert-characterised cases define a “fingerprint” in the representation space of a clinical sequence model. The fingerprint is then used to retrieve patients with similar trajectories in larger routine-care populations, before the condition is evident from diagnostic codes. Representations from autoregressive and JEPA-style models are to be compared with patient-similarity and weak-supervision baselines.

sections.title: Scientific discovery systems
sections.description: Making scientific literature and possible research directions easier to explore.

projects.title: NEXUS
projects.summary: Predicting where a method from one field could solve a problem in another, and testing the most promising candidates.
projects.aim: Many advances come from applying a method developed in one field to a problem in another, but these opportunities are mostly found by chance. NEXUS aims to learn from the history of such transfers to identify new, high-value method–problem combinations, and to record what happens when they are tested — including negative and untestable results — so that each cycle improves the next.
projects.approach: The unit of analysis is the first genuine application of a published method to a published problem, distinguished from papers that merely mention both. These events are mined from large, time-stamped literature corpora, and models trained only on information available before a cut-off date predict which new combinations are likely to occur and to be useful. Candidates are checked for novelty, tractable ones are tested in faithful experiments, and every outcome is kept in a ledger. Current work concentrates on reliable extraction of methods and problems from papers, starting in cardiovascular and other clinical domains.

projects.title: Physarum
projects.summary: Tools for mapping possible research directions around a project’s frontier and supporting scientific judgement.
projects.aim: When a research project reaches an uncertain point, the useful next step is rarely a single obvious task. Physarum aims to make that uncertainty explicit: to map plausible directions, record which were pursued and which were rejected, and help the researcher decide where to push next.
projects.approach: Named after the slime mould that finds efficient paths by extending and reinforcing exploratory tendrils, Physarum launches bounded groups of AI “scout” agents to explore the space around a project’s current frontier: methods, prior literature, risks and possible studies. Their findings are sorted into routes to pursue, verify, park or avoid, and kept as a persistent map, so that routes can be reinforced or retired as results come in. The researcher remains the decision-maker.

projects.title: glucose.ai
projects.summary: A public literature-discovery site connecting diabetes research with developments in AI and machine learning.
projects.aim: Research at the intersection of diabetes and artificial intelligence is spread across clinical journals, preprint servers and computer-science venues. glucose.ai aims to bring it together in one place that is current, searchable and easy to explore.
projects.approach: An automated pipeline collects new papers daily from PubMed, arXiv, bioRxiv, medRxiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar, removes duplicates, extracts full text where available and finds linked code repositories. Papers are embedded with a scientific-document language model to support semantic search, related-paper discovery and maps of the field. The collection holds more than 16,000 papers.

sections.title: Research software
sections.description: Software that helps research remain connected and usable over time.

projects.title: pi / Cog workflows
projects.summary: Tools for connecting research sources, experiments and synthesis, so useful work is easier to organise and revisit.
projects.aim: Long-running research involves many threads — papers, experiments, meetings, code and decisions — that are easy to lose. The aim is to keep them connected, so that work can be resumed, checked and built on.
projects.approach: Cog is a locally maintained knowledge base in which AI agents ingest sources, maintain linked summary pages, search curated literature collections and record project state, decisions and results with their provenance. It runs on open coding-agent tooling (pi) and supports structured workflows for literature review, planning, independent review of results and handover between work sessions.
